title: Choosing the Component: Seven for Red Cells, Ten for Platelets
summary: Match each blood component to what is missing, apply current red-cell and platelet thresholds (and the acute-MI exception), and recognise when the obvious product is wrong — HIT, antiplatelet brain bleeds, warfarin reversal and platelet refractoriness.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 41 Hit 5 (red-cell triggers), Hit 6 (platelet thresholds), Hit 7 (cryoprecipitate), Hit 22 (immune refractoriness), Trap 3 (platelets in HIT; PATCH) and Trap 5 (PCC vs plasma). Checked against Yang 2026, Mushtaq 2026, Li 2026, Coe 2026, Galli 2026, Rahe-Meyer 2026 and Hess 2026. Register flags: rv-acs-trigger (Hit 5, MINT), rv-cryo-trigger (Hit 7). Not taught: per-unit increments, the 100 × 10⁹/L CNS threshold, CCI < 7,500 cut-off, and platelets in ITP/TTP (no source read).

objectives: Match blood components to the deficit each replaces.
Apply restrictive red-cell thresholds and recognise the acute-MI exception.
Recognise when platelets or plasma are the wrong choice, and manage immune platelet refractoriness.

scenes.title: Four orders on the board — which one is wrong?
scenes.altText: A whiteboard with four transfusion orders: (1) 2 units RBC for a stable ICU patient with Hb 7.6 g/dL; (2) platelets for a patient with suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and no bleeding; (3) 4 units plasma to reverse warfarin before urgent surgery; (4) cryoprecipitate for a bleeding patient with fibrinogen 90 mg/dL. Question: “Which orders fit the evidence?”

cues.text: Four transfusion orders arrive at the blood bank at the same time.

Red cells for a stable ICU patient with hemoglobin seven point six. Platelets for suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Plasma to reverse warfarin. And cryoprecipitate for a bleeding patient with very low fibrinogen.
Only one of these clearly fits current evidence. Let’s see why.

props.label: ② Platelets · suspected HIT · not bleeding

scenes.title: Normal: each component replaces one thing
scenes.altText: Four cards in a row: Red cells → oxygen-carrying capacity; Platelets → primary hemostasis; Plasma → all coagulation factors, but dilute and large in volume; Cryoprecipitate → concentrated fibrinogen, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, factor XIII and fibronectin (AABB: ≥ 150 mg fibrinogen per unit). A banner: “Give the component that replaces what is missing — and only when the benefit outweighs the risk.”

cues.text: Every blood component replaces one thing. Red cells restore oxygen-carrying capacity.
Platelets support the first, platelet-plug stage of clotting.
Plasma contains all the clotting factors — but they are dilute, so large volumes are needed.

Cryoprecipitate is concentrated: fibrinogen, factor eight, von Willebrand factor and factor thirteen in a small bag. Each AABB-standard unit carries at least a hundred and fifty milligrams of fibrinogen.

props.label: Replace what is missing — when benefit > risk

scenes.title: What changes: thresholds, not reflexes
scenes.altText: Red-cell panel: restrictive threshold Hb 7 g/dL for most stable critically ill patients (trials showed no harm vs 9–10 g/dL); acute myocardial infarction is the exception — the MINT trial found a restrictive 7–8 g/dL strategy may increase MI or death, so a more liberal approach is favoured. Platelet panel (AABB 2025): prophylaxis < 10 × 10⁹/L in hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia; < 10 for compressible central line; < 20 for lumbar puncture; < 50 for major non-neuraxial surgery.

cues.text: Red cells: for most stable, critically ill patients, trials show a threshold of seven grams per decilitre is as safe as nine or ten.
Acute myocardial infarction is the exception. In the large MINT trial, a restrictive strategy of seven or eight may have increased heart attack or death, so many favour a more liberal approach there.
Platelets: prophylaxis below ten thousand per microlitre in stable hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia — and below ten for a central line at a compressible site.
Below twenty for a lumbar puncture, and below fifty for major surgery outside the spine and brain.

scenes.title: In the lab: when the obvious component is the wrong one
scenes.altText: Card 1, HIT: platelet transfusion is generally avoided because it can fuel immune activation and thrombosis; considered only for serious bleeding. Card 2, PATCH trial: platelets for intracerebral hemorrhage on antiplatelet drugs worsened outcomes. Card 3, warfarin reversal: vitamin K + 4-factor PCC is preferred — rapid INR correction in a small volume; plasma is slower, large in volume and an alternative only when PCC is unavailable. Card 4, refractoriness: poor platelet increments with HLA or platelet antibodies → crossmatch-compatible or HLA-selected platelets; non-immune causes → treat the cause. Card 5, cryo: fibrinogen falls early in major bleeding; bleeding risk rises below about 200 mg/dL (triggers vary).

cues.text: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: platelet transfusion is generally avoided, because it can fuel immune activation and clotting. It’s considered only for serious bleeding.
In the PATCH trial, giving platelets for brain hemorrhage in patients on antiplatelet drugs made outcomes worse.
To reverse warfarin quickly, give vitamin K with four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate. Plasma is slower, needs large volumes, and is a fallback only.
If platelet counts barely rise after transfusion and HLA or platelet antibodies are present, choose crossmatch-compatible or HLA-selected platelets. Non-immune causes are treated at the source.
And cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen, which falls early in major bleeding; risk rises below about two hundred milligrams per decilitre.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Low platelets + suspected HIT → give platelets” is crossed out → “Generally avoided unless serious bleeding.” Trap card: “Plasma is the fastest warfarin reversal” is crossed out → “Vitamin K + 4F-PCC.” Trap card: “Transfuse every ICU patient to Hb 10” is crossed out → “Restrictive 7 g/dL for most; acute MI is the exception.”

cues.text: Trap one: a low count in suspected HIT is not a reason to give platelets. They are generally avoided unless there is serious bleeding.
Trap two: plasma is not the fastest warfarin reversal. Vitamin K with four-factor PCC is.
Trap three: most stable ICU patients don’t need a hemoglobin of ten. A threshold of seven is standard — acute myocardial infarction is the exception.

scenes.title: Seven for red cells, ten for platelets
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Seven for red cells, ten for platelets — and ask what’s eating them.” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: seven for red cells, ten for platelets — and before you give platelets, ask what’s eating them.

Where it breaks: acute MI, active bleeding and procedures use different thresholds; trials and guidelines keep changing; and numbers never replace the clinical picture — a bleeding patient may need components at any count.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “RBC Hb < 7 for most stable patients (acute MI differs) · platelets < 10 prophylaxis, < 20 LP, < 50 major surgery”, “Avoid platelets in HIT · 4F-PCC for warfarin · cryo for fibrinogen · HLA/crossmatched for immune refractoriness”.

cues.text: Transfuse to evidence-based thresholds, not reflexes — seven for red cells in most stable patients, ten for prophylactic platelets — and choose the component that replaces what is missing.

props.label: RBC < 7 (acute MI differs) · platelets < 10 / 20 LP / 50 surgery
No platelets in HIT unless bleeding · 4F-PCC for warfarin · cryo for fibrinogen

explanation.what: Plain language: give the blood product that replaces what is missing, at evidence-based thresholds, and know the situations where the obvious product does harm. Scientific terms: restrictive RBC threshold Hb 7 g/dL in most stable critically ill patients; AABB 2025 platelet thresholds < 10 × 10⁹/L (hypoproliferative; compressible CVC), < 20 (LP), < 50 (major non-neuraxial surgery); cryoprecipitate supplies fibrinogen (≥ 150 mg/unit), FVIII, vWF, FXIII.
explanation.why: Trials show restrictive RBC strategies are as safe for most patients, but MINT suggested possible harm in acute MI. In HIT, transfused platelets can worsen immune activation and thrombosis; in PATCH, platelets worsened outcomes after antiplatelet-associated ICH. 4F-PCC delivers vitamin K-dependent factors rapidly in small volume.
explanation.measure: Hemoglobin, platelet count, fibrinogen; post-transfusion platelet increments (CCI) to detect refractoriness; HLA/platelet antibody testing guides crossmatch-compatible or HLA-selected platelets.
explanation.differs: Plasma (dilute, all factors, large volume) vs 4F-PCC (concentrated vitamin K-dependent factors) vs cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen-rich). Immune (antibody) vs non-immune platelet refractoriness.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: “which component?”, RBC and platelet thresholds, HIT/PATCH traps, PCC vs plasma, refractoriness management.

mnemonic.text: Seven for red cells, ten for platelets — and ask what’s eating them.
mnemonic.explanation: Hb 7 g/dL restrictive RBC threshold; platelet prophylaxis below 10 × 10⁹/L; consider consumptive or immune causes before giving platelets.
mnemonic.limitation: Acute MI, bleeding and procedures use different thresholds; guidelines change; bleeding patients may need components at any count.

analogyLimitations: Massive transfusion, neonatal thresholds and special products (irradiated, washed) are covered elsewhere or not at all.
takeaway: Transfuse to evidence-based thresholds, not reflexes — seven for red cells in most stable patients, ten for prophylactic platelets — and choose the component that replaces what is missing.

questions.stem: A stable ICU patient with sepsis (no cardiac disease, not bleeding) has Hb 7.6 g/dL. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: No red-cell transfusion now; transfuse if Hb falls below 7 g/dL
options.rationale: Correct. Restrictive thresholds are as safe as liberal ones in stable critically ill patients.

options.text: Transfuse 2 units to reach Hb 10 g/dL
options.rationale: Incorrect. Trials show no benefit of liberal targets in this group.

options.text: Give plasma to raise oxygen delivery
options.rationale: Incorrect. Plasma does not carry oxygen.
Incorrect. Cryo replaces fibrinogen, not red cells.

questions.stem: A patient on warfarin with INR 4.5 needs emergency surgery. Which is the preferred reversal?

options.text: Intravenous vitamin K plus 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate
options.rationale: Correct. 4F-PCC rapidly replaces vitamin K-dependent factors in a small volume.
Incorrect. Plasma is slower and needs large volumes; it is a fallback.
Incorrect. Platelets do not replace coagulation factors.
Incorrect. Cryo is a fibrinogen source, not a replacement for the vitamin K-dependent factors.

questions.stem: A hematology patient’s platelet count barely rises after several transfusions; HLA class I antibodies are detected. What should the blood bank provide?

options.rationale: Correct. Immune refractoriness responds to antibody-compatible platelets.

options.text: More random-donor platelets at double dose
options.rationale: Incorrect. Random platelets are destroyed by the antibodies.
Incorrect. Irradiation prevents TA-GVHD, not antibody-mediated destruction.
Incorrect. Plasma does not raise the platelet count.

references.usedFor: Curriculum source: scope and exam framing. Not used as verification.

references.citation: Yang H, Li F, Zhu Z, et al. Current perspectives and updates on transfusion strategies in critically ill anemic patients. Front Med (Lausanne). 2026;13:1762664.
references.usedFor: Restrictive 7 g/dL vs liberal 9–10 g/dL: no mortality difference in ICU and septic shock trials; 2023 AABB guidelines advocate restrictive thresholds; MINT (acute MI, n = 3504): restrictive 7–8 g/dL associated with more MI or death (HR 1.15).

references.citation: Mushtaq A, Salgado de la Mora M, Dabaliz AH, et al. The evolving landscape of platelet therapy: risks, innovations, and clinical judgment. Ann Hematol. 2026;105(1):14.
references.usedFor: AABB prophylactic thresholds: < 10 × 10⁹/L hypoproliferative (chemotherapy/allo-SCT), < 10 compressible CVC, < 20 lumbar puncture, < 50 major non-neuraxial surgery; PATCH trial — platelets for antiplatelet-associated ICH worsened outcomes.

references.citation: Li J, Wang L, Qin Y, et al. Personalized management of platelet transfusion refractoriness: risk factors, cross-matching, and IVIG strategies. Front Med (Lausanne). 2026;13:1923303.
references.usedFor: Immune refractoriness: crossmatch-compatible or HLA-selected platelets per guidelines; non-immune causes treated at source; CCI as the response measure.

references.citation: Coe B, Elkhashab I, Saldarriaga CA, Johnson D, Cattelino B. Clinical challenges in profound thrombocytopenia associated with type 2 heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT2). Cureus. 2026;18(3):e105848.
references.usedFor: Platelet transfusion is generally avoided in HIT because of immune activation and thrombosis risk; acceptable in serious bleeding.

references.citation: Galli M, Simeone B, Ten Berg J, et al. Managing bleeds on anticoagulant therapy: a practical guide for clinicians. Eur Heart J Acute Cardiovasc Care. 2026;15(7):557-572.
references.usedFor: VKA reversal: IV vitamin K + 4F-PCC preferred, rapid INR normalisation; plasma an alternative when PCC unavailable, limited by slower onset and large volumes.

references.citation: Rahe-Meyer N, Bartoszko J, Levy JH. Fibrinogen concentrate in acute hemorrhage: mechanistic insight, thresholds, and targeted replacement. J Clin Med. 2026;15(16):6156.
references.usedFor: Cryoprecipitate contains fibrinogen, FVIII, vWF, fibronectin, FXIII; AABB ≥ 150 mg fibrinogen per unit; fibrinogen often first factor to fall in major bleeding; bleeding risk increases below 200 mg/dL (varies by population).

references.citation: Hess AS, White SK, Crowe EP, et al. The clinical use of cryoprecipitate and fibrinogen concentrate: a scoping review. Transfusion. 2026;66(7):1424-1437.
references.usedFor: Trials commonly enrol bleeding patients with fibrinogen < 200 mg/dL; thawed conventional cryoprecipitate is usable for a limited time (thresholds and practice vary).

claims.text: Restrictive Hb 7 g/dL safe for most stable critically ill patients; MINT: restrictive 7–8 may increase MI/death in acute MI.
AABB platelet thresholds: < 10 hypoproliferative and compressible CVC, < 20 LP, < 50 major non-neuraxial surgery; PATCH harm.
Platelets generally avoided in HIT unless serious bleeding.
Vitamin K + 4F-PCC preferred over plasma for urgent warfarin reversal.
Immune refractoriness → crossmatch-compatible or HLA-selected platelets; non-immune → treat cause.
Cryo: fibrinogen (≥ 150 mg/unit AABB), FVIII, vWF, FXIII; bleeding risk ↑ below ~200 mg/dL fibrinogen.
Platelets relatively contraindicated in ITP and TTP; 1-h CCI < 7,500 on two occasions defines immune refractoriness.
